# Lucky Day (Doctor Who)

## Canonical Clarification and Production Details

The title "Lucky Day" refers to two distinct concepts within the fictional universe of *Doctor Who*. The primary subject of this report is the fourth episode of Doctor Who's fifteenth series (marketed globally as Season 2), an officially produced and broadcast television story [), )]. A separate, unreleased story concept with the same name exists as part of the expanded universe, written by Simon Guerrier but never developed into a television episode, audio drama, novel, or comic strip; it is documented only as a script concept in *Doctor Who Magazine Issue 620* . The televised episode is confirmed to be a completed and released installment of the Fifteenth Doctor's era, a fact supported by promotional appearances from cast members such as Millie Gibson on BBC's *The One Show*, who discussed the episode in the context of a season already underway . This report will focus exclusively on the canonical, broadcast version of "Lucky Day."

The episode was written by Pete McTighe and directed by Peter Hoar , , , . It was produced by Bad Wolf in association with BBC Studios, under the executive supervision of Russell T Davies, Julie Gardner, Jane Tranter, Joel Collins, and Phil Collinson . The producer for the episode was Vicki Delow . The musical score was composed by Murray Gold and performed by the BBC National Orchestra of Wales, conducted by Alastair King . The production design was handled by Phil Sims, while Pam Downe was the costume designer . Other key production personnel included Sam Care as director of photography, Ben Drury as editor, Andy Pryor CDG/CSA as casting director, Alex Thompson as sound recordist, Paul McFadden as re-recording mixer, Dave Houghton as VFX supervisor, and Julie Kendrick as hair & make-up designer . Post-production services were provided by Bang Post Production and Gorilla, with financial oversight led by Sean Kenneally and Mary Furlong from Bad Wolf, and John Hamer and Nick Lambon from BBC Studios .

"Lucky Day" premiered on Saturday, May 3, 2025 [), ), , )]. It aired on BBC iPlayer at 8:00 am BST and on BBC One later that evening in the United Kingdom . Globally, it was made available simultaneously on the Disney+ streaming platform , , . The episode forms Block Two of Series 15 alongside 'The Robot Revolution' and was filmed in Bristol, specifically at locations including Clifton and Frederick Place [), )]. Director Peter Hoar, who previously helmed the Eleventh Doctor-era episode 'A Good Man Goes to War', returned to the franchise for this installment, directing both 'Lucky Day' and 'The Robot Revolution' [, )].

## Narrative and Thematic Analysis

The narrative of "Lucky Day" is structured as a "Doctor-lite" episode, a format where the titular Time Lord, the Fifteenth Doctor portrayed by Ncuti Gatwa, appears only briefly at the beginning and end of the story [), ), ]. The central focus shifts entirely to companion Ruby Sunday, played by Millie Gibson, exploring her life and psychological state following her amicable departure from the TARDIS , . The episode delves deeply into themes of trauma, trust, and the difficulty of reintegrating into ordinary civilian life after experiencing extraordinary events . Ruby is depicted as struggling with symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), including emotional triggers and a profound inability to confide in others about her past for fear of being perceived as insane . Her journey serves as the emotional core of the narrative, which uses her relationship with a new character, Conrad Clark, as a catalyst for her growth and eventual processing of her experiences .

The story begins with Ruby attempting to build a normal life, only to have it disrupted by a mysterious creature stalking her . She meets Conrad, a conspiracy theorist whose belief in alien phenomena makes him uniquely receptive to her incredible claims [)]. Their relationship develops, providing Ruby with a safe space to share her memories of the Doctor and the wonders she witnessed . However, this burgeoning trust is shattered when Ruby suffers a "brutal gut-punch of a betrayal" upon discovering Conrad's true nature . He is revealed to be the leader of a radical activist group known as Think Tank, a collective of conspiracy theorists dedicated to discrediting government agencies like UNIT [), )]. This revelation marks a significant narrative pivot, transforming the initial character-driven drama into a high-stakes sci-fi thriller .

Conrad's motivation stems from a childhood encounter with the Doctor and UNIT personnel Belinda Chandra on New Year's Eve 2007, when the Fifteenth Doctor gave him a coin and told him, "it's your lucky day" [)]. This event planted the seed of his obsession, leading him years later to meticulously plan an operation to expose what he perceives as UNIT's lies [)]. His plan involves using Ruby, whom he has been secretly observing since their prior encounter with the Shreek monster ('Night of the Shreek'), to lure her to a public event in Colson in 2025 [, )]. There, he stages a fake attack by the alien creature, the Shreek, livestreaming the event to accuse UNIT of fabricating alien threats [)]. The episode incorporates modern social media culture through Think Tank's online campaign, using hashtags like #UNITLies and #DemandTheTruth to rally supporters and manipulate public opinion [)].

The climax of the episode sees Conrad infiltrate UNIT headquarters, assisted by a mole within the organization named Jordan Lang, doxxing multiple personnel and broadcasting their private information live [)]. In a final act of defiance against UNIT, he releases a real Shreek into the facility. The creature attacks him, but he refuses an offered antidote, choosing instead to die fighting before being dismembered [)]. This violent end, captured on the very livestream he initiated, provides undeniable proof of the alien threat, thereby reversing public perception and exposing the danger posed by Think Tank [)]. The Doctor returns at the conclusion of the episode, materializing inside a prison cell to confront Conrad and address the fallout, before departing again, allowing Ruby to continue her path forward [)]. Director Peter Hoar described the episode's tone as 'scary, surprising, and romantic', noting its evolution from an unassuming start to a high-octane thriller . He drew cinematic inspiration from classic *Doctor Who* serials like 'The Dæmons' and the film 'Aliens', aiming to blend gothic horror elements with contemporary conspiracy theory themes . Writer Pete McTighe confirmed that subtle clues were planted throughout the first half of the episode for attentive viewers, hinting at the impending twist involving Conrad's true allegiance .

## Characters and Worldbuilding

The episode centers on the return of several key characters and introduces new elements that significantly expand the *Doctor Who* universe. The protagonist, Ruby Sunday, is portrayed by Millie Gibson [), ]. Her arc explores the psychological aftermath of traveling with the Doctor, focusing on her struggle to find a place in the world without him . She is depicted as someone grappling with PTSD, finding it difficult to form connections due to the burden of her secret experiences . Her relationship with Conrad Clark serves as a crucial turning point, forcing her to confront her trauma and begin the process of moving forward .

Jonah Hauer-King plays Conrad Clark, a complex antagonist who initially presents as a sympathetic and understanding listener to Ruby's extraordinary stories [), ]. His character is driven by a fanatical belief system rooted in a childhood encounter with the Doctor, which he interprets as a personal calling [)]. As the leader of the radical conspiracy group Think Tank, Conrad orchestrates a sophisticated scheme to discredit UNIT, leveraging modern technology and social media to achieve his goals [), )]. His betrayal of Ruby is the central dramatic conflict of the episode, revealing him to be a manipulative and dangerous individual willing to sacrifice everything for his cause .

The episode also marks a significant return for the United Nations Intelligence Taskforce (UNIT). Kate Lethbridge-Stewart, portrayed by Jemma Redgrave, reappears as the head of the organization, overseeing its operations and response to the alien threat [), , )]. The story explores the internal workings of UNIT, highlighting its vulnerability to infiltration by a mole, Jordan Lang, who aids Conrad in his mission [)]. The narrative also introduces Anita Dobson as Mrs Flood and Varada Sethu as Belinda Chandra, who had a prior encounter with Conrad in 2007 [), )].

One of the most prominent additions to the show's lore is the Shreek, a new alien species designed by Gethin Alderman [)]. These creatures are characterized by their ability to project powerful pheromones, which can be used to track individuals [)]. Their vocalizations were brought to life by the voice actor Nicholas Briggs, known for his work on numerous *Doctor Who* monsters [)]. The Shreek serve as both a genuine threat and a tool for manipulation in the hands of Think Tank, representing a gothic horror-inspired menace [, )].

Furthermore, "Lucky Day" establishes important continuity links with previous episodes. It references Conrad's earlier sightings of the Doctor and Ruby at Chez Alison, a location from the episode 'The Runaway Bride' [)]. It also shows photos of the TARDIS from 'Fear Her' (during the 2012 Olympics) and 'Aliens of London' (the London UFO crash), reinforcing the Doctor's long history of presence on Earth [)]. The story also makes a nod to the broader expanded universe by having Ruby mention the Shreek in relation to the 2024 BBC New Series Adventures novel 'Caged' [)]. Structurally, the episode is identified as containing a "Halfway Plot Switch," a narrative device that signals a major shift in the story's direction . Critically, it is paired with '73 Yards,' the fifth episode of the following season, suggesting a deliberate, long-term planning strategy across back-to-back filmed seasons to create parallel narrative arcs . Finally, the episode sets up future developments, notably establishing connections to 'The Robot Revolution' and prompting UNIT to take drastic action, such as relocating the Osterhagen Project after it becomes compromised [), ), )].

## Reception and Critical Response

The reception of "Lucky Day" was highly polarized, presenting a stark contrast between the creative enthusiasm during its production and its performance upon broadcast. During pre-production, the episode generated significant excitement. The script read-through was described by writer Pete McTighe as "the most rowdy Doctor Who read through I've ever been to," characterized by audible gasps from the audience, indicating strong creative buy-in and anticipation . Director Peter Hoar lauded the episode as 'scary, surprising, and romantic,' highlighting its ambitious blend of genres and its potential for a rewarding viewing experience, especially for those who pay close attention to the subtle clues woven into the narrative , . This positive sentiment suggests that the creative team viewed the "Doctor-lite" format and the complex character dynamics as a successful and innovative approach to storytelling.

However, upon its release on May 3, 2025, the episode's critical and audience reception proved to be controversial. Multiple sources reported that "Lucky Day" became the lowest-viewed and lowest-rated episode in the show's 62-year history [)]. Specifically, it garnered only 1.5 million overnight viewers, a figure that signaled a significant disconnect with the viewing public [)]. This poor performance raises questions about how the episode was received by the wider audience compared to the high praise it received internally.

Several factors could account for this discrepancy between creator intent and audience reaction. Firstly, the "Doctor-lite" format may have confused or failed to attract a segment of the target demographic that expects a full-throttle adventure featuring the Doctor as the central hero. By sidelining the lead character for much of the runtime, the episode shifted its focus away from traditional *Doctor Who* formula, potentially alienating viewers accustomed to that structure [), ]. Secondly, the heavy thematic focus on contemporary conspiracy theories and Ruby's psychological struggles with PTSD might have felt overly bleak or thematically dissonant to some viewers. The narrative's exploration of paranoia, manipulation, and the brutal betrayal of a close friend could have been perceived as unnecessarily harsh or emotionally taxing without the Doctor's presence to provide perspective, comfort, or a more fantastical resolution [), ]. Thirdly, a marketing failure cannot be ruled out. If the promotional materials did not adequately communicate the episode's unique "Doctor-lite" premise, they may have set misleading expectations, leading to disappointment among viewers who anticipated a different kind of story.

In summary, while the creators and production team clearly invested significant effort into crafting a nuanced and thrilling standalone story centered on a companion's emotional journey, the episode's reception highlights a potential gap between artistic ambition and mainstream audience appeal. Its low ratings represent a notable moment of controversy within the ongoing series, sparking discussion about the viability of shifting focus away from the Doctor and the effectiveness of addressing modern socio-political anxieties within the established *Doctor Who* framework. The dichotomy between the enthusiastic production environment and the tepid public response makes "Lucky Day" a compelling case study in the complexities of television storytelling and audience engagement.

## Legacy and Associated Media

Despite its controversial reception, "Lucky Day" left a lasting impact on the Fifteenth Doctor's tenure and remains a significant entry in the series' recent history. The episode successfully explored the long-term consequences of time travel on a companion's mental health, a theme that resonated with many fans . It also demonstrated a willingness to experiment with narrative structure by adopting a "Doctor-lite" format, paving the way for future installments to explore similar character-centric approaches [), )]. The introduction of the Shreek and the conspiracy group Think Tank added new layers to the show's mythology, expanding the range of threats beyond traditional monsters and establishing a more grounded, contemporary political dimension to UNIT's operations [), )]. The episode's structural parallelism with '73 Yards' from the subsequent season also indicates a sophisticated, long-term planning strategy by the writing team, creating interconnected narratives that span multiple stories .

The legacy of the episode is further solidified through its availability in various formats. It is included on Disc Three of the official Season 2 Blu-ray box set, titled 'Disc Three' . This box set was released in the United Kingdom on August 18, 2025, and is available in multiple physical formats, including Steelbook, Blu-ray, and DVD . Retailers such as HMV, Rarewaves, and Amazon stock the set, ensuring broad accessibility for collectors and home viewers . The release includes exclusive special features that provide deeper insight into the production process. These features include a 'Lucky Day - Making of' documentary and a 'Lucky Day – Scene breakdown with Peter Hoar,' allowing fans to analyze the director's vision and the technical execution of the episode . This inclusion in the official home media release ensures that the episode is preserved and celebrated as part of the canonical broadcast series.

To conclude, "Lucky Day" stands as a pivotal and divisive chapter in the revival era of *Doctor Who*. While its low viewership numbers marked a challenging moment for the show, its bold narrative choices, deep character work, and expansion of the series' world have cemented its importance. The episode's exploration of trauma and trust, combined with its innovative structure and memorable antagonists, contributes to the rich tapestry of the Fifteenth Doctor's adventures. Through its availability on Blu-ray with detailed behind-the-scenes content, its legacy continues to be accessible to fans, inviting new analyses and discussions about its place in the long-running science fiction series.

May 06, 2025

Pete McTighe, the man behind the fourth episode of Season 2, discusses the latest instalment of Doctor Who and its forthcoming spin-off, _The War Between the Land and the Sea_...

[_Lucky Day_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/lucky-day) sees the return of former companion [Ruby Sunday](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/ruby-sunday) and her allies at UNIT as they face an all-new threat. The episode also welcomes back writer Pete McTighe to the Whoniverse, previously known for his work on [Thirteenth Doctor](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/thirteenth-doctor) adventures [_Kerblam!_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/kerblam) and [_Praxeus_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/praxeus). McTighe is the showrunner on the forthcoming Doctor Who spin-off series featuring UNIT, _The War Between the Land and the Sea_ - but more on that later.

We spoke to Pete about his experiences writing the episode, being on-set for filming, the inspiration behind characters like [Conrad Clark](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/conrad-clark), as well as what’s next for [Kate Lethbridge-Stewart](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/kate-lethbridge-stewart) and UNIT. Spoilers for _Lucky Day_ below!

_**Lucky Day**_ **is now streaming on BBC iPlayer in the UK and Disney+ where available.**

![Image 1: Pete McTighe Interview](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV_PeteMcTighe2-87b295811a.jpg)

Pete McTighe with the TARDIS on set of 'Lucky Day'.

_**Welcome back to the Whoniverse! How did your involvement in Season 2 come about?**_

When Russell took over as Doctor Who showrunner, we Facetimed and he told me he’d love to have me back at some stage, which was such an exciting prospect – we’ve known each other for years and worked together on a show that hasn’t seen the light of day yet (one day!) Eventually, the stars aligned and we discussed an idea for an episode that focused on the character of Ruby which of course became _Lucky Day_.

I think we had a 45-minute initial chat over Zoom, because I was on holiday in Australia at the time. Russell was incredibly generous and gave me a huge amount of freedom to take the idea and run with it… this was in 2023, before the 60th specials had aired, before anything of the [Fifteenth Doctor](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/fifteenth-doctor) had been seen yet. So to prep for writing the script, I had this amazing week, where I was sent twelve brand new episodes of Doctor Who to watch starring David Tennant and Ncuti Gatwa. I watched two a day, it was bliss! And obviously I was paying particular attention to Ruby Sunday and how Millie was embodying that role.

After that, the script was written pretty quickly, Russell was happy and we were off! The episode was shot in the first recording block of the season late that year, alongside [_The Robot Revolution_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-robot-revolution).

![Image 2: Lucky Day Gallery](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-04/DWTV-Gallery-LuckyDay7-79747f709a.jpg)

**Lucky Day** _**follows Ruby Sunday in her post-TARDIS life. How has she changed as a character since parting ways with the Doctor?**_

What I love about this story is that it examines Ruby from a place of utterly real psychological truth. You absolutely would have PTSD after everything she went through in her first season. You’d be triggered by all sorts of things. You’d not be able to confide in anyone, cos they’d think you were insane. All those mind-blowing events she experienced kind of had to be shut away in a box and not talked about – because she also had some other, very personal, mind-blowing things to deal with, like forming a relationship with her birth parents. I mean, that’s a lot.

So for Ruby, meeting someone in Conrad who she feels she can open up to and share her experiences with, that’s such a relief for her. And, obviously, such a brutal gut-punch of a betrayal when it turns out he’s been playing her. I feel like Ruby’s grown up a lot since we left her, but during this episode she grows up even more, she finally comes to terms with the psychological impact that last year had on her, takes ownership of that trauma, and starts to move on with her life.

![Image 3: Pete McTighe Interview](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV_PeteMcTighe4-725c2b02f5.jpg)

_**UNIT’s greatest challenge in this episode is facing public distrust and misinformation. What inspired the rise of Think Tank?**_

Well, I mean look around. We’re living in a crazy world where misinformation has become currency and distrust is rife. That speech I wrote for the Doctor at the end of the episode – he says everything I wanted to say. I refer you to the Doctor.

And for classic fans, yes, ‘Think Tank’ is a deliberate call-back to the story [_Robot_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/robot) from 1975. I figured Conrad did his research, and stole the name of a previous organisation that opposed and clashed with UNIT.

![Image 4: Pete McTighe Interview](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV_PeteMcTighe7-9edfe85093.jpg)

_**How enjoyable was it to write a villain like Conrad Clark, and what was it like working with guest star Jonah Hauer-King?**_

I loved writing Conrad. It was delicious, knowing where the story was going and being able to relish the lead-up to that reveal. The episode was structured very deliberately into three acts with a genre change at every major turn; a rom-com first, then a gothic horror, then a contemporary thriller. What a gift, to be able to switch genres like that in a single episode. But the character dictating those swings of genre was Conrad, and he had to be absolutely believable at every turn.

Getting Jonah to play the role was just a dream; I mean, the man’s a film star. I was dubious that we’d get him but we sent him the script, and lucky for us he loved it and came onboard very quickly. He was so perfect, and such a fantastic presence on set. To see him step into a terrifying machine like Doctor Who with such confidence, skill, preparation and enthusiasm was just a joy to watch. He and Millie worked so hard, and were so committed to bringing the best out of this story.

![Image 5: Pete McTighe Interview](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV_PeteMcTighe3-4f94f17ccb.jpg)

Pete (middle) on-set with Jonah Hauer-King (Conrad) and Millie Gibson (Ruby).

_**You were on set for every day of filming – any stories to tell?**_

Oh lots, but here’s my favourite… we were shooting the big climactic UNIT Ops Room scene, where the helipad doors open and the [Shreek](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-shreek)’s containment unit is revealed. Which meant we needed big wind machines. So in they came, these huge industrial fans. At the right moment, the technicians turned them on, a massive gust of wind ripped through the set… and suddenly, it was raining rose petals! All those long-forgotten red petals from the dance sequence in [_The Giggle_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-giggle) had been stuck in the studio rafters for over a year and came drifting down into the set. It was hilarious, like the [Toymaker](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-toymaker) was still haunting us. Jemma Redgrave, bless her, scooped up a pocketful and handed them to me after the scene as a memento. I’ve kept them.

Oh, and on the actual 60th anniversary, 23rd November 2023, we were on set in the [TARDIS](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/the-tardis), shooting the big showdown between the Doctor and Conrad. Russell made a speech and we had a giant police-box cake. What a day, it was like Christmas for me.

![Image 6: Pete McTighe Interview](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV_PeteMcTighe1-3cc5f5e6ff.jpg)

Pete's salvaged rose petals from the UNIT set!

_**We also get to see a little bit more of how UNIT operates in the absence of the Doctor. What’s different about writing a Doctor Who story with more of an ensemble cast?**_

I actually really enjoyed writing a story where the Doctor was largely absent, I surprised myself. Because instantly, when he’s not around, the stakes are higher. The situation is way more dangerous if he’s not there to swoop in and save the day. It means ordinary people – like Ruby, like Kate – have to become extraordinary in the face of impossible challenges.

I mean, look at the extremes that Kate is driven to by the end of the episode. Her entire organisation – her father’s legacy – was under threat, and not a threat they’re used to. This wasn’t the Kraals - but something much more dangerous and insidious and damaging. And how we leave her in this episode, and at the end of the season, really sets her up for what’s to come in _The War Between the Land and the Sea_.

![Image 7: Pete McTighe Interview](https://cms.doctorwho.tv/sites/default/files/2025-05/DWTV_PeteMcTighe5-ce82642c08.jpg)

_**As well as your work on the TV series and**_ **The War Between the Land and the Sea**_**, some of your writing credits within the greater Whoniverse include**_ **Tales of the TARDIS** _**and some very special features for the Collection! Which characters from Doctor Who history have been your favourite to write for?**_

Every one of those projects has been a dream come true. Literally, since I was five, I’ve been imagining Doctor Who TV stories. I have a bank of hundreds of them, probably. Doctor Who is so incredibly rich when it comes to its history and its characters, so it’s impossible and unfair to pick a favourite.

I love writing Kate Lethbridge-Stewart, but also [Ace](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/ace). Also [Vicki](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/vicki). Also [Leela](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/leela). Also the Mara, the [Daleks](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/daleks), the [Seventh Doctor](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/seventh-doctor), the Thirteenth, The Fifteenth. [Mel](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/mel-bush)! [Nyssa](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/nyssa)! [Shirley](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/shirley-bingham)! [Christofer Ibrahim](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/colonel-christofer-ibrahim). [Jamie](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/jamie-mccrimmon) and [Zoe](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/zoe-heriot). Ruby, [Belinda](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/belinda-chandra). But I also love writing the new; Conrad, and [Cherry Sunday](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/cherry-sunday) and [Mrs Flood](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/mrs-flood) and brilliant characters yet to be announced for _The War Between_. And more to come if Russell will have me back – I love the history of Doctor Who with all my heart, but I’m excited by the future, the stories we haven’t told yet.

* * *

**Pete McTighe will return to the Whoniverse as writer and showrunner of forthcoming spin-off** _**The War Between the Land and the Sea**_ **–** [**find out everything we know here**](https://www.doctorwho.tv/news-and-features/everything-we-know-so-far-about-doctor-who-spin-off-the-war-between-the-land-and)**.**

5.content:
**Warning: contains spoilers for _Doctor Who_ episode “Lucky Day”.**

As the Doctor and Belinda work to find their way back to 2025, we catch up with previous companion Ruby Sunday and her new boyfriend, the very nice, normal and unproblematic Conrad. Meanwhile, having previously triumphed against Daleks, Autons, Cybermen and rogue Time Lords, UNIT faces its most dangerous enemy yet – podcasters. Spoilers ahead.

A creative challenge born of production necessity, so-called [‘Doctor-lite’ episodes](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-doctor-lite-stories-ranked/) – in which the title character is marginalised in some way to keep budgets down and free up the lead actor’s schedule – are inevitably about the absence of the Doctor. What happens to the misfits and oddballs who don’t get to travel in the TARDIS? What if the Doctor died and never had the chance to change the companion’s life? How might a companion deal with the Doctor’s sudden disappearance?

The second Doctor-lite episode to focus on Ruby Sunday (Millie Gibson) after last year’s ambitious, divisive “[73 Yards](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-series-14-episode-4-review-73-yards/)“, ‘Lucky Day’ finds a new variation on the concept – what does a companion do when they’ve amicably parted ways with the Doctor and have to go back to normal life, armed with all that amazing, terrifying knowledge? We’ve seen the idea poignantly explored through classic series companion Sarah Jane Smith in the Tenth Doctor episode “School Reunion”, though the Doctor was very much involved there, whereas here Ruby has only recently left the TARDIS, and under very different circumstances. It’s still a potent idea – in theory. But despite a typically committed and engaging performance from Gibson, the episode struggles to find a compelling take on it.

Part of the issue is that Ruby seems pretty together, all things considered. She’s got her gran and two loving mums (three if you count Kate Lethbrige-Stewart, as Shirley points out in one of the episodes’s best lines). She’s tentatively pursuing a new relationship, which is arguably a healthy thing to do, even if this particular one doesn’t exactly end well. Even her ‘fight or flight’ state of mind, which she ascribes to PTSD, is well founded and isn’t shown to be disrupting her daily life – she’s not constantly jittery, finding aliens and monsters round every corner. All we really see is her responding to an elaborate prank in a way that feels completely logical given her experience.

Unfortunately, this ends up undermining the emotional throughline of the story. What is Ruby’s character arc meant to be? Seeking out others with some understanding of her experiences makes sense, and the episode doesn’t seem to be suggesting that she is trying to fill the Doctor-shaped hole in her life in an emotionally unhealthy way. Conrad seeming like a bit of a Doctor fanboy is the only real red flag, but he’s sweet and attentive otherwise, and you can see why she falls for him. So while her monologue at the end of the episode about needing to be on her own for a while certainly makes sense as a reaction to what she’s been subjected to by Conrad, it doesn’t really feel like a payoff to what’s set up at the beginning.

Which brings us to Conrad himself. In a way, Conrad is a more successful version of the villain the show tried to give us in “[The Robot Revolution](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-series-15-episode-1-review-the-robot-revolution/)“, though the misogyny is more subtextual here. The performance is much stronger, which helps, and Jonah Hauer-King effectively sells Conrad’s mid-point heel turn with that casually malevolent “nailed it”. The twist is pretty effective, as it initially seems like Conrad’s Doctor obsession is what’s going to drive a wedge between him and Ruby – it’s certainly a better example of subversion than the show inadvertently coming out as pro-Amazon in “[Kerblam!](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-series-11-kerblam-review/)“, also written by Pete McTighe.

However, once the episode has pivoted to show Conrad’s true colours, it runs into the curious problem of being simultaneously too specific and too general. In the hellscape that is 2025, we are unfortunately far too aware of the various types being explored here – the amoral grifter exploiting people’s insecurities, the true believer conspiracist soaking in dangerous misinformation, and the furious reactionary driven to commit terrible acts of violence. The problem is, the episode can’t seem to decide which of these types it wants Conrad to be, so it tries to make him all three, which doesn’t really work. Not because there could never be any crossover between those types, but because the episode doesn’t have the time (or, seemingly, the inclination) to dramatise the progression.

So by the time Conrad is breaking into UNIT, stealing a gun and shooting people, it’s hard to parse his true motivations. Is it about money and self promotion? Is it revenge because they didn’t give him a job? Has he actually started to believe his own hype? During his climactic conversation with the Doctor, which Hauer-King plays with cold psychopathy, I was half convinced he was going to turn out to be [the Master](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-ranking-the-master-stories-which-is-the-best/), publicly speed running online radicalisation for a laugh. There’s a version of this that could have worked – feinted at with comically underdeveloped UNIT stooge Jordan – where Conrad’s thoughtless grifting ends up radicalising somebody else into doing something horrific, but having one character embody every facet of the issue just ends up making him feel inconsistent.

The uneasy balancing act of translating these topical real-world dynamics to the world of _Doctor Who_ also applies more broadly to the episode’s engagement with conspiracies, disinformation and online witch hunts. I’m generally of the mindset that it’s wise not to get _too_ invested in continuity and canon when it comes to a 60-year-old show in which time travel is a major factor, but it’s difficult not to wonder how, in a world that has seen so many alien invasions, the anti-UNIT meme could take off so fast and have such immediate and catastrophic ramifications. Governments overreacting to public opinion and doing something stupid? Believable! People convincing themselves that a world-shaking event – like, I dunno, a pandemic – didn’t actually happen? Also believable! But in the context of this specific fictional universe, it just raises a few too many distracting questions.

Based on all this, you might be thinking that the episode is a dog’s breakfast, but there’s good stuff in here! As stated, [Millie Gibson](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-millie-gibson-ruby-has-to-be-her-own-hero-73-yards/) is great, even if she’s not always best served by the writing – her pain at Conrad’s betrayal feels raw and tangible, and her climactic “go to hell” is satisfying. Shirley’s dry sense of humour is always welcome, and as with “[73 Yards](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-series-14-episode-4-review-73-yards/)“, it feels like the show has finally found the best use for Jemma Redgrave as Kate. She works really well as a mentor figure for Ruby, both actors believably selling the affection between the two, and the moment where she shouts “Don’t you _dare_ point a gun at her” hits hard. Kate taking things too far with Conrad and the Shreek is also dramatically compelling, especially as everyone around her seems visibly uncomfortable. It feels like an interesting new angle for the character, and something that could put her on a collision course with the Doctor.

And while the Doctor-Conrad confrontation does feel a bit like McTighe (or, one suspects, an uncredited Russell T Davies) turning directly to camera to deliver a rant, it’s hard not to feel some satisfaction when Ncuti Gatwa gives the guy both barrels. More steely, seething contempt from this Doctor please, he’s rather good at it.

Overall, then, an interesting if messy experiment with lots of compelling ideas, even if doesn’t ultimately hang together. Engaging with the current moment is something _Doctor Who_ is going to need to do if the show is to remain relevant – though hopefully in future that engagement will be a bit more deft.

_[Doctor Who](https://www.denofgeek.com/doctor-who/) continues with “The Story and The Engine”_ _on Saturday May 10 on BBC One and iPlayer in the UK, and on Disney+ around the world._

Doctor Who Director, Peter Hoar, Describes Lucky Day as “Scary, Surprising, and Romantic”
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 1: Doctor Who Director, Peter Hoar, Describes Lucky Day as “Scary, Surprising, and Romantic”](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Lucky-Day-Millie-Gibson-Ruby-Sunday.jpg)

*   Posted On: [3 May 2025](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/2025/05/03/doctor-who-director-peter-hoar-describes-lucky-day-as-scary-surprising-and-romantic/)
*   Posted By: [Philip Bates](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/author/prbates36/)
*   Comments: [0](https://thedoctorwhocompanion.com/2025/05/03/doctor-who-director-peter-hoar-describes-lucky-day-as-scary-surprising-and-romantic/)

One of my favourite directors, Peter Hoar, returns to _Doctor Who_ with _Lucky Day_, and the BBC has released a lovely interview with Hoar in which he enthuses about coming back to the franchise.

Hoar last helmed _A Good Man Goes to War_ with the Eleventh Doctor (Matt Smith), but has since directed productions like _Cloak & Dagger, The Last of Us, Daredevil, Cipher, Shetland,_ and _It’s A Sin_. This time around, he’s working with Ncuti Gatwa, aka the Fifteenth Doctor…

**You directed an episode of _Doctor Who_ in 2011. What was it like to return?**

It was fantastic. I had my good friends around me and a very positive, exciting new world to discover. I have also changed as a director, and I felt so much more confident. But my love for the show has never diminished.

**What can audiences expect from this episode?**

The episode is quite a journey from its unassuming beginning to high octane sci-fi thrill ride. We had many references for this episode from all kinds of cinema and TV including Devil’s End from _The Dæmons_ to _Aliens_.

**This episode has lots of familiar faces including the UNIT team. What was it like working with them?**

It was a joy! They are all superb without question. Watching them face such an extreme foe as this, then working as a team, being pushed to the edge, seeing their humanity tested to its limits… I hope will make a great episode. The cast worked so hard to bring this to life and deserve huge praise. I particularly like one shot where the three women of UNIT stand shoulder to shoulder.

**This episode sees the return of Ruby Sunday (Millie Gibson), and Jonah Hauer-King joins the cast as Conrad, what can you tease about the dynamic between the pair?**

Jonah and Millie were a great duo. Jonah fitted so smoothly into the family, and it was exciting to watch a new fresh dynamic emerge. Ruby needs a new hero and Conrad thinks he’s all that, but we discover quickly that it’s Ruby who’s better in a dangerous situation…

**We know that this episode takes us back to the UNIT Tower. What is it like being on that set?**

It’s a huge place with a lot of visual promise. It led me to make a new pitch for the end sequence that we had a lot of fun shooting. We threw everything at them. Literally!

**There is a terrifying monster in this episode, what was it like bringing it to life on camera?**

Would it be _Doctor Who_ without a monster? This one is genuinely scary. And we leant right in to it – one scene in particular we went full gothic horror.

**If you could travel in the TARDIS to any time and place in the universe, where would you go?**

The distant future as far away as possible

**How would you sum up this episode?**

Scary, surprising, and romantic.

**_Lucky Day_ is available later today (3rd May 2025) via BBC iPlayer and Disney+, and airs on BBC1 tonight.**
