_[Doctor Who](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/DoctorWho "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/DoctorWho")_ examples of stories with [uncanny similarities](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RecycledScript "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RecycledScript") to older ones.

* * *

*   ["The Gunfighters"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS3E8TheGunfighters "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS3E8TheGunfighters") has the same plot as ["The Myth Makers"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS3E3TheMythMakers "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS3E3TheMythMakers"), both by the same writer. A comedic historical story where the Doctor is mistaken for a historical figure (Zeus/Doc Holliday) and through a series of farcical events, people die.
*   Not only is ["The Moonbase"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E6TheMoonbase "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E6TheMoonbase") a [Sequel Episode](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SequelEpisode "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SequelEpisode") to ["The Tenth Planet"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E2TheTenthPlanet "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E2TheTenthPlanet"), it rehashes the same plot, just replace the South Pole with the Moon and the subplot involving the space capsule in danger with one about a mysterious illness.
*   "[Spearhead from Space](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS7E1SpearheadFromSpace "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS7E1SpearheadFromSpace")" was based on a story that [Robert Holmes](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes") wrote for the film _Invasion_, which featured an alien crashing in the woods near a rural hospital, where a medical examination reveals his alien nature. The hospital is later visited by other aliens, seeking a fugitive criminal. Some of the exact lines of dialogue used by human doctors to describe the physiology of the injured alien were re-used, which ended up creating the defining two-hearted feature of Time Lord anatomy in the process (while also giving viewers familiar with the one-hearted First Doctor something to scratch their heads over).
*   ["Day of the Daleks"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS9E1DayOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS9E1DayOfTheDaleks") was apparently a rush adaptation from _[The Outer Limits](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/TheOuterLimits1963 "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/TheOuterLimits1963")_ script "Soldier".
*   [Terry Nation](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/TerryNation "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/TerryNation") rehashed "[The Daleks](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS1E2TheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS1E2TheDaleks")" for "[Planet of the Daleks](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS10E4PlanetOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS10E4PlanetOfTheDaleks")". It contains some of the same plot devices, including: a group of Daleks in a city encountering the Thals on a ravaged planet; a deadly plague instead of a neutron bomb; someone using a Dalek shell as a disguise; the Doctor imprisoned in a cell and with paralysed legs (albeit in "The Daleks" it was Ian whose legs were paralysed); and the Daleks imprisoned in their city at the end of the story.
*   For "[Robot](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS12E1Robot "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS12E1Robot")", [Terrance Dicks](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/TerranceDicks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/TerranceDicks") drew on _[The Avengers](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/TheAvengers1960s "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/TheAvengers1960s")_ episode "The Mauritius Penny", which he co-wrote with [Malcolm Hulke](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/MalcolmHulke "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/MalcolmHulke"), most notably for the scenes in which Sarah Jane infiltrates the meeting of the Scientific Reform Society.
*   Both ["The Android Invasion"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E4TheAndroidInvasion "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E4TheAndroidInvasion") and ["The Brain of Morbius"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E5TheBrainOfMorbius "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E5TheBrainOfMorbius") — two consecutive serials! — feature a genius [Mad Scientist](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MadScientist "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MadScientist") who treats bodies like playthings and has a complex about creation and destruction, and a more sympathetic assistant who was rescued from a spaceship accident by the scientist and is missing a body part, who does a [Heel–Face Turn](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeelFaceTurn "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HeelFaceTurn") upon discovering that the body part was actually accounted for all along. Part of this was because both scripts had to be heavily edited by [Robert Holmes](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes"), who wrote most of the material between Styggron and Crayford in "The Android Invasion" to pad out the run time, and who adapted "The Brain of Morbius" to feature a mad scientist/[The Igor](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheIgor "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheIgor") pair to [reduce the required budget](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BottleEpisode "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BottleEpisode"); presumably he'd had this dynamic on the brain.
*   The story ["The Seeds of Doom"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E6TheSeedsOfDoom "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E6TheSeedsOfDoom") (by Robert Banks Stewart) was recycled from _[The Avengers](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/TheAvengers1960s "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/TheAvengers1960s")_' "Man-Eater of Surrey Green". (Stewart had written for _The Avengers_, but not that episode, which was by Philip Levene.) "The Seeds of Doom" feels wrong for a _Doctor Who_ story in many ways, since it follows the _Avengers_ formula. For example, the Fourth Doctor casually jumps on top of a bad guy and punches him out!
*   The Doctor is coerced into leading his companions on a key [Fetch Quest](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FetchQuest "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/FetchQuest"), which takes them to a wide variety of locales. Among the obstacles encountered are a [Kangaroo Court](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KangarooCourt "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KangarooCourt") trial at which one of them is sentenced to death. Upon completion of their mission, they must _not_ turn the found items over to the one who demands them. Is this the First Doctor tracking down the [Keys of Marinus](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS1E5TheKeysOfMarinus "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS1E5TheKeysOfMarinus"), or the Fourth [looking](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E1TheRibosOperation "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E1TheRibosOperation") [for](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E2ThePiratePlanet "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E2ThePiratePlanet") [the](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E3TheStonesOfBlood "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E3TheStonesOfBlood") [Key](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E4TheAndroidsOfTara "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E4TheAndroidsOfTara") [to](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E5ThePowerOfKroll "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E5ThePowerOfKroll") [Time](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E6TheArmageddonFactor "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E6TheArmageddonFactor")?
*   For his first script "[The Visitation](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS19E4TheVisitation "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS19E4TheVisitation")", [Eric Saward](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/EricSaward "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/EricSaward") recycles the premise and basic plot beats of [Robert Holmes](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes")' "[The Time Warrior](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS11E1TheTimeWarrior "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS11E1TheTimeWarrior")".
*   "[Enlightenment](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS20E5Enlightenment "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS20E5Enlightenment")" has a similar plot to that of "[The War Games](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS6E7TheWarGames "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS6E7TheWarGames")": both involve aliens abducting humans from various points in Earth history and using them for their own ends.
*   "[The King's Demons](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS20E6TheKingsDemons "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS20E6TheKingsDemons")" has a similar plot to "[The Time Meddler](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS2E9TheTimeMeddler "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS2E9TheTimeMeddler")", in that they both involve Doctor trying to stop one of his own people trying to alter history.
*   The Fifth Doctor story ["Warriors of the Deep"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS21E1WarriorsOfTheDeep "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS21E1WarriorsOfTheDeep") bears striking similarities to the final First Doctor story, ["The Tenth Planet"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E2TheTenthPlanet "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E2TheTenthPlanet"). Both feature the Doctor and his companions accidentally arriving at an isolated military base and being mistaken for spies, and in both stories the Doctor's warnings go unheeded until the base is besieged by an alien threat. In both there is a section of the story where the alien invaders seize the bridge and the Doctor is forced by circumstances to stand by without interfering for a time.
    *   Writer Johnny Byrne drew inspiration from the _[Space: 1999](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/Space1999 "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Series/Space1999")_ episode "Guardian of Piri", which he script-edited.
*   For "[The Two Doctors](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS22E4TheTwoDoctors "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS22E4TheTwoDoctors")", [Robert Holmes](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/RobertHolmes") reused the idea of villains trying to steal the Doctor's genetic code from his unused script for "[The Five Doctors](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho20thASTheFiveDoctors "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho20thASTheFiveDoctors")". Originally it was the Cybermen, now it was the Sontarans.
*   In many ways, Holmes' penultimate story, "[The Mysterious Planet](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS23E1TheMysteriousPlanet "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS23E1TheMysteriousPlanet")", is a bigger budget remake of his first story, "[The Krotons](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS6E4TheKrotons "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS6E4TheKrotons")".
*   Holmes' final story, ["The Ultimate Foe"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS23E4TheUltimateFoe "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS23E4TheUltimateFoe"), repeats the plot of his earlier story ["The Deadly Assassin"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS14E3TheDeadlyAssassin "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS14E3TheDeadlyAssassin"): The Doctor has been brought to Gallifrey and is put on a sham trial for a crime he didn't commit, which turns out to be the result of a renegade Time Lord with a personal connection to him tampering with the seemingly infallible Matrix and conspiring with Gallifreyan politicians to achieve power and prolong his life (the Valeyard acting as a [Composite Character](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CompositeCharacter "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CompositeCharacter") of both Chancellor Goth and the Peter Pratt version of the Master). The Doctor chases him into the Matrix, where, despite being at a huge disadvantage, he defeats him in a battle of wits and walks away a free man, but not before the renegade escapes and sneaks off to cause more mayhem.
*   For "[Time and the Rani](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS24E1TimeAndTheRani "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS24E1TimeAndTheRani")", [Pip and Jane Baker](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/PipAndJaneBaker "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/PipAndJaneBaker") drew upon their 1986 _Find Your Fate_ book _Race Against Time_, in which the Rani tries to build a Time Destabiliser in order to reshape the universe to her design.
*   "[Silver Nemesis](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS25E3SilverNemesis "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS25E3SilverNemesis")" received some complaints that it was the same basic plot as "[Remembrance of the Daleks](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS25E1RemembranceOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS25E1RemembranceOfTheDaleks")" (earlier in the very same season). Both concerned the Doctor arranging events so that he was ready to destroy an invasion of Earth by some of his deadliest enemies using an ancient piece of Time Lord technology (that the enemies themselves had hoped to gain control of). Both stories also feature themes of bigotry and racial purity, and a group of humans who naïvely try to ally themselves with the alien invaders.
*   ["Fear Her"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E11FearHer "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E11FearHer") itself is very similar to ["The Idiot's Lantern"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E7TheIdiotsLantern "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E7TheIdiotsLantern") from the same season. Both feature an alien who imprisons people during a major televised event in London (the Queen's Coronation and the Olympic Games) and a child with an abusive father. In both, at the climax, one of the protagonists falls victim to the alien, and the other must rescue them before time runs out. "Fear Her" was written in a hurry to replace a [Stephen Fry](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/StephenFry "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/StephenFry")\-penned script that ultimately went unproduced, which could explain the recycling process. It would then go on to be recycled _twice_:
    *   ["Night Terrors"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS32E9NightTerrors "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS32E9NightTerrors"): A child in an everyday contemporary Earth environment turns out to be an alien whose reality-warping powers cause his fears to threaten his family and neighbours. [When did we see that before?](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E11FearHer "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E11FearHer")
    *   ["Flatline"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E9Flatline "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E9Flatline"): The antagonists can turn two-dimensional things into three-dimensional ones and vice versa. The Doctor ends up trapped by them and can only assist his female companion from afar in protecting others and ensuring his return, whereupon he sends the antagonists back where they came from. The main difference is that the "Flatline" antagonists, the Boneless, are malicious rather than misguided-but-sympathetic.
*   ["Smith and Jones"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E1SmithAndJones "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E1SmithAndJones") gets its plot recycled for ["The Eleventh Hour"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E1TheEleventhHour "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E1TheEleventhHour"). Both involve an alien convict with shapeshifting powers escaping to Earth and a group of alien police threating to kill innocent people if they cannot find it in a certain amount of time. This requires the Doctor and his new companion to find it first. Additionally, the Doctor's sonic screwdriver is destroyed at one point and a hospital is a major setting.
*   [Chris Chibnall](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/ChrisChibnall "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/ChrisChibnall") recycles ["Planet of Evil](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E2PlanetOfEvil "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS13E2PlanetOfEvil") in his first new series script, ["42"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E742 "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E742"). Like Planet of Evil, it involves the crew of a spaceship mining a sentient body for a fuel source. The celestial body wants it back, and possesses people in order to sabotage the ship. Only difference? The Doctor is possessed too.
*   ["Victory of the Daleks"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E3VictoryOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E3VictoryOfTheDaleks") borrows big chunks of the [lost serial](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MissingEpisode "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MissingEpisode") ["The Power of the Daleks"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E3ThePowerOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E3ThePowerOfTheDaleks"), but with more of a knowing, [Internal Homage](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InternalHomage "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/InternalHomage")/[Whole-Plot Reference](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WholePlotReference "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WholePlotReference") approach. The stuff that's borrowed — Daleks feigning servitude to humans, the Doctor protesting that they're pure evil and no-one believing him, a quirky scientist who discovered them promoting them to the leader of his people as a new development that can solve all of their problems, the Daleks doing it all as a plan to grow their ranks — is all aesthetic stuff, and the actual plot machinery itself is fairly different. For example, "Power" takes place on a human colony on another planet, "Victory" is set in WWII London.
*   ["The Curse of the Black Spot"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS32E3TheCurseOfTheBlackSpot "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS32E3TheCurseOfTheBlackSpot") (Eleventh Doctor) uses almost exactly the same [Twist Ending](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TwistEnding "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TwistEnding") as ["The Empty Child"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E9TheEmptyChild "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E9TheEmptyChild")/[The Doctor Dances"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E10TheDoctorDances "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E10TheDoctorDances") (Ninth Doctor), revealing that the [Monster of the Week](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MonsterOfTheWeek "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MonsterOfTheWeek") was actually just medical software for an abandoned alien ship, and that its actions were the result of it blindly following its programming and trying to heal injured humans without understanding human physiology. The plot even involves a young boy's relationship with a distant parent that he barely knows. It takes place in [The Golden Age of Piracy](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/TheGoldenAgeOfPiracy "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/TheGoldenAgeOfPiracy") instead of [World War II](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/WorldWarII "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/UsefulNotes/WorldWarII"), and the monster is a [siren](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OurSirensAreDifferent "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OurSirensAreDifferent") instead of a zombie, but the plots are otherwise exactly the same.
*   The Minisodes ["Meanwhile in the TARDIS 2"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E5FleshAndStone "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E5FleshAndStone") and ["Clara and the TARDIS"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS33ShortClaraAndTheTardis "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS33ShortClaraAndTheTardis") are both virtually identical accounts of the Eleventh Doctor's companion getting the TARDIS to show them a slideshow of former companions (with the male ones conspicuously missing) and show comical disgust at the Doctor's [perceived womanising](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheCharmer "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheCharmer"), as well as his ["typical male" interests in machines and women, with the implication that the TARDIS is doing it out of female jealousy](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GenderDynamicsIndex "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/GenderDynamicsIndex"). "Clara and the TARDIS" also swipes scenes from the [Red Nose Day special](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2011RNDSSpaceAndTime "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2011RNDSSpaceAndTime") where multiple Amys get stuck in a time loop and flirt with each other, when multiple Claras get stuck in a time loop and flirt with each other.
*   ["Deep Breath"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E1DeepBreath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E1DeepBreath"), the Twelfth Doctor's debut story:
    *   The basic plot is sort of a [Darker and Edgier](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DarkerAndEdgier "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/DarkerAndEdgier") version of the Fourth Doctor's first story, ["Robot"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS12E1Robot "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS12E1Robot"), which [Steven Moffat](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/StevenMoffat "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/StevenMoffat") mentioned using as a reference — with the A and B-plots swapped. The Doctor regenerates and suddenly develops an absolutely crazy and seemingly uncaring personality that disconcerts his companion(s) and the people his previous self works with ("Robot" B-plot, "Deep Breath" A-plot, with Clara's discomfort central to the story) while a robot with an [ambiguously humanlike personality](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RidiculouslyHumanRobots "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/RidiculouslyHumanRobots") and [psychological complexes mirroring the Doctor's own](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PlotParallel "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/PlotParallel") is responsible for some bizarre murders ("Robot" A-plot, "Deep Breath" B-plot). The Doctor's defeat of it is rather ambiguous as a happy ending, but the companion agrees to give the new Doctor a chance to befriend her — after a bit of talking to from the Doctor. Several lines and setpieces from "Robot" were lifted into "Deep Breath" to indicate the similarities: Vastra quotes one of the Brigadier's lines apropos of nothing, and the Twelfth Doctor's white nightgown is similar to how the Fourth Doctor is dressed in the infirmary.
    *   The minisode playing before it in cinemas shows Strax giving a Field Report to the audience about all of the previous faces the Doctor has had, with funny descriptions of their personalities, to assuage an audience needing a reminder that the Eleventh Doctor was not always the Doctor — a format previously used for one of the "Strax's Field Report" online minisodes. The introduction is repeated almost word-for-word, although Jenny and Vastra interrupt it in the cinema version. Few of the _jokes_ are recycled, though — Strax's opinions on the other Doctors (not to mention which gender he thinks they are) are completely different between both minisodes.
*   ["The Caretaker"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E6TheCaretaker "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E6TheCaretaker") is largely a retread of ["The Lodger"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E11TheLodger "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E11TheLodger") - both stories are [breather episodes](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BreatherEpisode "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BreatherEpisode") in which [the Doctor goes undercover - badly - as a regular human,](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HughMann "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HughMann") in order to apprehend an alien threat. Indeed, both episodes take as their title the identity the Doctor assumes. The stories had the same writer.
*   ["Dark Water"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E11DarkWater "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E11DarkWater")/["Death in Heaven"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E12DeathInHeaven "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E12DeathInHeaven"), the Series 8 finale, combines the central plots of two previous season finales: ["Army of Ghosts"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E12ArmyOfGhosts "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E12ArmyOfGhosts")/["Doomsday"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E13Doomsday "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS28E13Doomsday") in Series 2 and ["The Sound of Drums"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E12TheSoundOfDrums "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E12TheSoundOfDrums")/["Last of the Time Lords"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E13LastOfTheTimeLords "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS29E13LastOfTheTimeLords") in Series 3. In Series 2, beings that are assumed to be the souls of deceased humans turn out to be Cybermen planning an invasion of Earth via a parallel universe; Series 8 has deceased humans being tricked into letting their consciousnesses and remains become the basis for a Cyber-army. In both Series 3 and 8, a recurring background character is revealed to have been a regeneration of the Master all along, planning to wipe out humanity with an army of robotic minions — leading to a pivotal scene aboard an airborne UNIT base where "The President" holds court as Earth's representative. Replace ghosts with skeletons, "Mr. Saxon" with "Missy", the Toclafane with the Cybermen, _Valiant_ with "Boat One", and the President of the United States with the President of Earth! All three stories also end with the Doctor and his current companion parting ways under unhappy circumstances, but that's par for the course for NewWho season finales; notably, all three companions are reunited with the Doctor sometime afterward.
*   ["Heaven Sent"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS35E11HeavenSent "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS35E11HeavenSent") draws upon the classic series serials ["The Deadly Assassin"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS14E3TheDeadlyAssassin "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS14E3TheDeadlyAssassin"), in which a companion-less Doctor is trapped in a nightmare world and pitted against an implacable, deadly foe for a lengthy stretch, and ["Castrovalva"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS19E1Castrovalva "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS19E1Castrovalva") in that said world (the city of Castrovalva/a mysterious castle) is the creation of an enemy and capable of shifting and changing its form, leaving the Doctor to figure out a way to escape before he's destroyed. In addition, the villains in both stories turn out to be Time Lords. But much as "Deep Breath" focuses more on its characters and their emotional states than "Robot" did, "Heaven Sent" is at heart a tragic character study of the Doctor instead of a conventional adventure. The reason he is companion-less is not because he couldn't take her with him to where he is, but because she is dead, meaning his mood is _much_ different than in "The Deadly Assassin". Save for one scene he's the only character who has dialogue, and the episode is only about him trying to survive and escape the isolated location — there's no villain for him to defeat, only a monster to run from, and he doesn't confront the party responsible for his torment until the next episode.
    *   Aside from those, there's an apparently heavy influence from [Steven Moffat](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/StevenMoffat "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/StevenMoffat")'s favourite [Sixth Doctor](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/ColinBaker "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/ColinBaker") episode, Rob Shearman's ["The Holy Terror"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/BigFinishDoctorWho014TheHolyTerror "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/BigFinishDoctorWho014TheHolyTerror"), which _also_ features the Doctor trapped in an [Epiphanic Prison](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EpiphanicPrison "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/EpiphanicPrison") shaped like an immense castle [with no outside](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WorldLimitedToThePlot "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/WorldLimitedToThePlot"), in which events eternally reset and recur. The only major differences being the Twelfth Doctor is alone, and he, not another character, is the prisoner.
*   ["The Lie of the Land"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E8TheLieOfTheLand "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E8TheLieOfTheLand") borrows a lot from past episodes. The Doctor and Bill recruit a group of soldiers to [take down a group of aliens](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LaResistance "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/LaResistance") with religious connotations that also shoot lightning like in ["The Wedding of River Song"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS32E13TheWeddingOfRiverSong "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS32E13TheWeddingOfRiverSong"), the villain using a network of mind control devices to control and rule humanity — and the plan to turn it against them — plus the setup of the companion needing to save the Doctor while the villains have control of Earth first happened in the Series 3 finale, and the companion stopping the villains thanks to the memory of her deceased mother (with the fact that the memory is not real being important) comes from ["The Rings of Akhaten"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS33E7TheRingsOfAkhaten "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS33E7TheRingsOfAkhaten").
*   The Master's plan in season ten involves creating a Cyberman army. A black character who is relevant throughout the series is [Killed Off for Real](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KilledOffForReal "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KilledOffForReal") and then reborn as a Cyberman while the companion goes though [Break the Cutie](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BreakTheCutie "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BreakTheCutie") as a result. Now, are we talking about ["Dark Water"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E11DarkWater "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E11DarkWater")/["Death in Heaven"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E12DeathInHeaven "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS34E12DeathInHeaven") or ["World Enough and Time"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E11WorldEnoughAndTime "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E11WorldEnoughAndTime")/["The Doctor Falls"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E12TheDoctorFalls "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS36E12TheDoctorFalls")? The main differences are Clara's love interest is converted and her [Break the Cutie](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BreakTheCutie "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/BreakTheCutie") is due to grief in "Dark Water", while it is the companion herself who is converted and being forced to take [The Slow Path](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheSlowPath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheSlowPath") while separated from the Doctor and getting Cyber-converted is what breaks her in "World Enough and Time". Plus, there are two Masters running around in the latter, with one flipping sides. Thinking it through, some of this is intentional: after Saxon regenerates into Missy offscreen, she tries his plot again with what's left behind from it but with a more — to her way of thinking — positive end in mind than he did. She'll fail, and eventually make her way to this point only to die because she forced him to regenerate, bringing her story tragically full circle.
    *   Also, a common complaint about the denouement was that it meant that two of the Twelfth Doctor's companions had virtually the same final fate. Both Clara Oswald and Bill Potts end up staving off death by becoming immortal or close enough to it, leave with another immortalized woman to travel the universe for more adventures, and neither bid the Doctor a proper final goodbye due to him being amnesiac of them/apparently dead at the time, meaning he doesn't know until the end of his incarnation what actually became of them. It's even more similar for those who ship Clara and Ashildr/Me, as Bill and Heather are canonically lovers.
*   ["Arachnids in the UK"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS37E4ArachnidsInTheUK "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS37E4ArachnidsInTheUK"), like ["The Green Death"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS10E5TheGreenDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS10E5TheGreenDeath"), has mutated invertebrates caused by the illegal dumping of toxic waste into a mineshaft by a [Corrupt Corporate Executive](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CorruptCorporateExecutive "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/CorruptCorporateExecutive").
*   "[The Battle of Ranskoor Av Kolos](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS37E10TheBattleOfRanskoorAvKolos "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS37E10TheBattleOfRanskoorAvKolos")" inolves an evil alien targeting planets and compressing them into small balls that they keep on display. This was the premise of "[The Pirate Planet](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E2ThePiratePlanet "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS16E2ThePiratePlanet")".
*   ["Resolution"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2019NYSResolution "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2019NYSResolution") is one to 2005's "[Dalek](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E6Dalek "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS27E6Dalek")". Both episodes reintroduce the Daleks to the series after a period of absence, by showing how menacing and dangerous a single pepperpot could be. They start with a single Dalek damaged and contained, but unintentionally allowed to restore itself by human technology. Both Daleks manipulate humans to further their escape, and kill large numbers of soldiers in their way. They interface with human information technology, demonstrate flight capabilities, and are eventually [destroyed by fire](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KillItWithFire "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/KillItWithFire").
    *   There are also similarities to Gareth Roberts' novella _I am a Dalek_, in which a deactivated Dalek is found in an archaeological dig, and a young woman falls under its influence as it restores itself.
*   ["Revolution of the Daleks"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2021NYSRevolutionOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWho2021NYSRevolutionOfTheDaleks") takes elements from "[The Power of the Daleks](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E3ThePowerOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS4E3ThePowerOfTheDaleks")" (humans attempting to utilize what they assumed are harmless Daleks for their own purposes, one among them being an obsessed scientist the Daleks maniuplate and then killed) and ["Victory Of The Daleks"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E3VictoryOfTheDaleks "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS31E3VictoryOfTheDaleks") (The humans' intent to develop a Dalek-based defence system for the British government.)
    *   The second half of the episode homages "The Evil of the Daleks" and the Daleks trilogy arc in the [John Nathan-Turner](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/JohnNathanTurner "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Creator/JohnNathanTurner") era in a civil war occurring between pure Daleks and their impure kin. "Remembrance of the Daleks" also had the two Dalek factions shooting it out on the streets of London.
*   [The Reveal](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheReveal "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/TheReveal") in ["Empire of Death"](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath") plays very similar to two previous seasons' [Myth Arcs](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MythArc "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/MythArc"). Namely, a godly entity whose powers derive from the Time Vortex spreads a meme through time and space to draw the Doctor and his companion to a certain spot (like the Bad Wolf in Series 1), and said meme takes the form of a woman reappearing as a different person each time (like Clara Oswald in Series 7). Only this time, it's the [Arc Villain](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcVillain "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/ArcVillain")'s plot instead of what saves the day at the end.
*   The Fifteenth Doctor's two seasons, having been filmed almost back-to-back, have many parallels between them. Each episode from one season can be paired with its counterpart from the other season, going by episode number:

1.  "[Space Babies](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E1SpaceBabies "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E1SpaceBabies")" & "[The Robot Revolution](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E1TheRobotRevolution")": A light, campy season opener which is the most classically sci-fi episode of the season, and with a major AI character who is later revealed to be a human (Nan-E and the AL Controller respectively).
2.  "[The Devil's Chord](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E2TheDevilsChord "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E2TheDevilsChord")" & "[Lux](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E2Lux")": The Doctor faces against a member of the Pantheon of Discord in a mid-20th century setting, with the plot revolving around a form of popular entertainment (respectively, music and motion pictures).
3.  "[Boom](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E3Boom "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E3Boom")" & "[The Well](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E3TheWell "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E3TheWell")": A "grittier" episode with a supporting cast of [Space Marines](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpaceMarines "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/SpaceMarines") and plot points calling back to previous episodes by the same scriptwriters.
4.  "[73 Yards](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E473Yards "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E473Yards")" & "[Lucky Day](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E4LuckyDay "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E4LuckyDay")": A "Doctor-lite" episode focusing on Ruby Sunday with a [Halfway Plot Switch](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HalfwayPlotSwitch "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/HalfwayPlotSwitch") and an appearance by Kate Stewart and UNIT.
5.  "[Dot and Bubble](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E5DotAndBubble "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E5DotAndBubble")" & "[The Story & the Engine](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E5TheStoryAndTheEngine "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E5TheStoryAndTheEngine")": Less blatant than the others, but both episode's mysteries revolve around missing people, the topic of racism in relation to the Fifteenth Doctor's racial appearance is tackled, and a character (Ricky September/The Barber) serves as a [Foil](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Foil "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/Foil") to the Doctor, even having a "companion" of his own.
6.  "[Rogue](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E6Rogue "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E6Rogue")" & "[The Interstellar Song Contest](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E6TheInterstellarSongContest "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E6TheInterstellarSongContest")": An [Affectionate Parody](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AffectionateParody "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/AffectionateParody") of a popular televised show, with the Doctor almost [Jumping Off the Slippery Slope](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JumpingOffTheSlipperySlope "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/JumpingOffTheSlipperySlope") when he believes his oath of protection towards his companion to have been broken.
7.  & 8. "[The Legend of Ruby Sunday](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E7TheLegendOfRubySunday "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E7TheLegendOfRubySunday")"/"[Empire of Death](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS40E8EmpireOfDeath")" & "[Wish World](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E7WishWorld "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E7WishWorld")"/"[The Reality War](https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E8TheRealityWar "/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Recap/DoctorWhoS41E8TheRealityWar")": The two-part finale featuring the return of a long-unseen foe from the classic series, now mutated into a giant, more monstrous form and heralded by the same woman who has mysteriously been reappearing all throughout the season, and with the main companion gaining an unexpected family member at the end.

Doctor Who Season 2 episode titles revealed
===========================================

March 21, 2025

Share:

Get ready for eight all-new adventures with the Doctor and Belinda from 12th April 2025!

As the TARDIS gets set to land on 12th April 2025, the episode titles for Season 2’s epic interstellar adventures have been revealed. The highly anticipated simultaneous global launch will kick-start with _The Robot Revolution_ at 8am exclusively on BBC iPlayer and later that day on BBC One in the UK. Those outside of the UK can watch exclusively on Disney+ (where available).

[**Discover everything we know about Season 2 here.**](https://www.doctorwho.tv/news-and-features/everything-we-know-about-doctor-who-season-2)

Find out the upcoming episode titles below...

### Doctor Who – Season Two | Episode Titles

*   [_The Robot Revolution_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-robot-revolution): Written by Russell T Davies, directed by Peter Hoar  
     
*   [_Lux_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/lux): Written by Russell T Davies, directed by Amanda Brotchie  
     
*   [_The Well_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-well): Written by Russell T Davies & Sharma Angel Walfall, directed by Amanda Brotchie  
     
*   [_Lucky Day_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/lucky-day): Written by Pete McTighe, directed by Peter Hoar  
     
*   [_The Story & the Engine_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-story-and-the-engine): Written by Inua Ellams, directed by Makalla McPherson  
     
*   [_The Interstellar Song Contest_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-interstellar-song-contest): Written by Juno Dawson, directed by Ben A. Williams  
     
*   [_Wish World_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/wish-world): Written by Russell T Davies, directed by Alex Sanjiv Pillai  
     
*   [_The Reality War_](https://www.doctorwho.tv/stories/the-reality-war): Written by Russell T Davies, directed by Alex Sanjiv Pillai

New episodes will debut weekly with an array of dazzling guest cast including Emmy Award winner Alan Cumming as cartoon foe [Mr Ring-a-Ding](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/mr-ring-a-ding), as well as Rose Ayling-Ellis, Anita Dobson, Bonnie Langford, Jemma Redgrave, Ruth Madeley, Susan Twist, Caoilfhionn Dunne, Christopher Chung, Evelyn Miller, Ariyon Bakare, Julie Dray, Michelle Greenidge, Angela Wynter, Alexander Devrient, Rylan, Freddie Fox, Jonah Hauer-King, Kadiff Kirwan and many more.

Russell T Davies, Showrunner said: “Excitement mounts as the new season gets closer, and there's nothing a Doctor Who fan loves more than facts! So here’s a whole bunch of them, with titles and writers, everything you need to get ready for transmission!”

**Doctor Who returns on Saturday 12th April with** _The Robot Revolution_**, available on BBC iPlayer and BBC One in the UK and Disney+ where available.**

Story partially missing
Note: Due to _Shada_ being affected by [BBC](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/BBC "BBC") industrial action around the time it was filming, the story was never completed and ended up being unbroadcast. * An attempt to remake the story was made on [4 February](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/4_February_/(production/) "4 February (production)") [1992](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/1992_/(production/) "1992 (production)"), with the footage being stitched together with linking narration from [Tom Baker](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Tom_Baker "Tom Baker"), as himself, and released on [BBC Video](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/BBC_Video "BBC Video") on [6 July](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/6_July_/(releases/) "6 July (releases)") [1992](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/1992_/(releases/) "1992 (releases)"). * [Big Finish Productions](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Big_Finish_Productions "Big Finish Productions") remade the story as [WC](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/WC "WC"): _[Shada](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Shada_/(webcast/) "Shada (webcast)")_ with [Paul McGann](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Paul_McGann "Paul McGann")'s [Eighth Doctor](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Eighth_Doctor "Eighth Doctor") on [12](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/12_November_/(production/) "12 November (production)") and [14 November](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/14_November_/(production/) "14 November (production)") [2002](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/2002_/(production/) "2002 (production)") and released from [2 May](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/2_May_/(releases/) "2 May (releases)") to [6 June](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/6_June_/(releases/) "6 June (releases)") [2003](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/2003_/(releases/) "2003 (releases)"). An exclusive adaption in the form of [AUDIO](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/AUDIO "AUDIO"): _[Shada](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Shada_/(audio_story/) "Shada (audio story)")_ was released on [21 November](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/21_November_/(releases/) "21 November (releases)") 2003. * In [2011](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/2011_/(production/) "2011 (production)"), [Ian Levine](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Ian_Levine "Ian Levine") privately funded animation to fill in the gaps in the already existing parts of the story. [Paul Jones](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Paul_Jones "Paul Jones") was hired to fill in for Baker, who declined to appear. Levine hoped for an agreement with [BBC Worldwide](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/BBC_Worldwide "BBC Worldwide") for a commercial release on [DVD](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/DVD "DVD"). This never materialised. * An attempt to recreate the story with animation was made with recording taking place from [9](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/9_July_/(production/) "9 July (production)") to [13 June](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/13_July_/(production/) "13 July (production)") [2017](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/2017_/(production/) "2017 (production)"). Who)") Episodes began being filmed in HD from _Planet of the Dead_. Unusual to the show, a series of five specials were featured following the series finale _Journey's End_ to compensate for the lack of an actual series in the year between this and the following series: two [Christmas Specials](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Christmas_Special "Christmas Special"), an [Easter Special](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Easter_Special "Easter Special"), an [Autumn Special](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Special#Autumn "Special") and a [New Year Special](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/New_Year_Special "New Year Special"). The second Christmas Special and the New Year Special marks the first time since [Season 26](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Season_26 "Season 26") that a multi-parter is labelled under one title. These specials were generally considered by the production team at the time to be part of the preceding Series 4, being specifically coded "4.X". David Tennant considered _Planet of the Dead_ to be "Episode 15". The specials were broadcast on a [Thursday](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Thursday "Thursday"), [Saturday](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Saturday "Saturday"), The special was broadcast on a [Tuesday](https://tardis.fandom.com/wiki/Tuesday "Tuesday"). _on_ [August 16, 2025](https://downthetubes.net/final-seventh-doctor-lost-story-headlines-new-doctor-who-magazine/ "6:28 am")

The latest issue of **_Doctor Who Magazine_** – Issue 620 – heads back to the 1990s with its cover story, as a lost Seventh Doctor adventure, _**Alixion**, by_ **Robin Mukherjee**, is revived as an audio drama.

![Image 1](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/img_7722-723x1024.jpg)

![Image 2](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/img_7733-768x1024.jpg)

_The regular and subscription copy covers of Doctor who Magazine 620_

The release, Sylvester McCoy again playing the mysterious Time Lord, is the final adaptation of stories that were being considered for _Doctor Who_’s “Season 27” back in 1989, before the show went on “hiatus”, effectively cancelled by the BBC without ever making any official announcement to that effect at the time.

Although new _Doctor Who_ projects are in progress the irony that the future of the TV series is currently in the balance will not have escaped regular readers of the title.

![Image 3](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/img_7724-1024x1024.jpg)

[The audio release of _Alixion_ next month](https://www.bigfinish.com/releases/v/doctor-who-alixion-3173), originally intended as the Seventh Doctor’s final regular story, means all the adventures developed to some extent for Season 27 have now finally been released.

_Bad Destination_, by Ben Aaronovitch, has been released as _Earth Aid_; _Thin Ice_, by Marc Platt, has been released under its own title; as have _Action at a Distance_, released as _Crime of the Century_, and _Blood and Iron_ as _Animal_, stories by Andrew Cartmel.

The Season 27 Big Finish audio dramas form part of the company’s long-running **_[Doctor Who – The Lost Stories](https://www.bigfinish.com/ranges/v/doctor-who---the-lost-stories)_** series, launched back in 2009.

Over the last twenty five years, **[Robin Mukherjee](https://www.robinmukherjee.com/robinmukherjee.com/Home.html)**’s work has stretched from art house cinema – in the esoteric tradition of Satyajit Ray – to mainstream television. Along the way he has written for radio and theatre and directed for both theatre and television.  He has also taught extensively, and has recently been appointed as a Lecturer in Scriptwriting at Bath Spa University.

![Image 4](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/image-2.jpg)

_A scene from “His Mad Pranks” by Alan Barnes and Martin Geraghty_

While the magazine’s focus is the show itself, it’s great to see the comic strip – “**His Mad Pranks**” in full swing, a romp of a Fifteenth Doctor tale by **Alan Barnes** with art by **Martin Geraghty**, set during the most recent TV season. Events are about to come to a head as the Doctor discovers the true identity of a mysterious foe, only to find there is a much more dangerous one lurking in the wings. Martin is at the top of his game on this story’s art, and you’ll enjoy the reveal!

If you’re a fan of the strip, don’t forget the latest collection, **_The Monster Makers_**, is out soon, and a special variant cover limited edition by **David Roach** is available to preorder now exclusively from the publisher’s web store. **[Read our full story about that release here](https://downthetubes.net/dont-miss-out-on-doctor-who-the-monster-makers-variant-edition/)**!

**_• Doctor Who Magazine Issue 620 is on sale now in all good newsagents, some run by Zygons, and comic shops, too – [or](https://doctorwhomagazine.com/doctor-who-magazine/doctor-who-magazine-620/) [if’s](https://doctorwhomagazine.com/doctor-who-magazine/doctor-who-magazine-620/) [sold out, order direct from Panini UK here](https://doctorwhomagazine.com/doctor-who-magazine/doctor-who-magazine-620/), don’t be blue!_**

**• [Check out _Doctor Who: The Monster Makers_ Variant Cover Edition here on the Panini online store](https://www.panini.co.uk/shp_gbr_en/doctor-who-the-monster-makers-gbdrg039-uk02.html)**

**• _Doctor Who: The Monster Makers_ Regular Edition is available from 2nd September 2025 | ISBN: 978-1804913024 | B[uy it from AmazonUK (Affiliate Link)](https://amzn.to/4m0MiL2)**

In Issue 620 of Doctor Who Magazine…
------------------------------------

![Image 5](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/img_7729-797x1024.jpg)

_Lee Binding’s cover art for Doctor Who: The Collection Season 13_

*   _Zygons! Sutekh! Kraals! Krynoids!_ An enjoyable exploration of **_Doctor Who: The Collection Season 13_** Blu-ray box set. Including: details of a documentary on Ian Marter who played companion Harry Sullivan, producer Phillip Hinchcliffe visiting the locations from the series, and the creation of new monster effects

![Image 6](https://downthetubes.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/img_7735.jpg)

_[Lew Stringer](https://lewstringercomics.blogspot.com/2025/08/zygons-go-daft.html) pokes fun at Season 13’s Zygons in his “Daft Dimension” strip, described by one fan as “the best part of the magazine”_

*   Enter the Black Archive! Join _Doctor Who_’s brand manager James Page in San Diego as he takes fans behind the scenes at this year’s Doctor Who activation.
*   Props art director **Michael van Kesteven** talks us through the creation of various gadgets for this year’s season, including: colour variants of the Doctor’s sonic, the “Polish! Polish!” robot Scoot, and the Rani’s time ring bracelet
*   The Seventh Doctor in Ukraine! Dalek and Cyberman performer Mickey Lewis recounts how he joined Sylvester McCoy on a journey to entertain fans in war-torn Kyiv.

*   A lost Seventh Doctor adventure! TV writer **[Robin Mukherjee](https://www.robinmukherjee.com/robinmukherjee.com/Home.html)** talks to _DWM_ about working on _Doctor Who_ in the 1980s and how his story _Alixion_ has finally been realised as an audio drama…
*   An entertaining royal audience with **Mary Reynolds**, who made an enjoyable cameo as the late Queen Elizabeth in the 25th anniversary serial _Silver Nemesis_
*   After Image: **[Simon Guerrier](https://0tralala.blogspot.com/)** looks back at _Lucky Day_, _The Story & the Engine_, _the Interstellar Song Contest_ and _Wish World_/_The Reality War_
*   Find out how students across the UK’s universities are testing their _Who_ knowledge with a challenging quiz league
*   Back to 1975 (and 1963): Giving life to the Loch Ness Monster
*   The Randomiser: **Gary Gillatt** offers a fascinating look into the war service of William Hartnell, Patrick Troughton and Jon Pertwee, who played first three TV Doctors
*   _DWM_ examines the hidden depths of _Dark Water_, in the first part of a Fact of Fiction feature on the finale to the Twelfth Doctor’s first season.

**Regular features**

*    Gallifrey Guardian: _DWM_’s news round-up including the announcement of a new range of adventures – across books, comics, audio and the web – that will reveal more about Jo Martin’s Fugitive Doctor
*   Reviews – featuring the latest audio and book releases
*   Other Worlds – the essential guide to new stories in _Doctor Who_’s expanded universe
*   Prizes to be won – including the new _Monster Makers_ Comic Collection from Panini!

John  is the founder of downthetubes, launched in 1998. He is a comics and magazine editor, writer, and Press Officer for the [Lakes International Comic Art Festival](https://www.comicartfestival.com/). He also runs [Crucible Comic Press](https://downthetubes.net/crucible-press/).

Working in British comics publishing since the 1980s, his credits include editor of titles such as _Doctor Who Magazine_ and _Overkill_ for Marvel UK, _Babylon 5 Magazine, Star Trek Magazine_, and its successor, _Star Trek Explorer_, and more. He also edited the comics anthology _STRIP Magazine_ and edited several audio comics for ROK Comics; and has edited several comic collections and graphic novels, including volumes of “Charley’s War” and “Dan Dare”, and [_Hancock: The Lad Himself_](https://amzn.to/42W3wm3), by Stephen Walsh and Keith Page.

He’s the writer of  comics such as _Pilgrim: Secrets and Lies_ for B7 Comics; “Crucible”, a creator-owned project with _2000AD_ artist Smuzz; and “Death Duty” and “Skow Dogs”, with Dave Hailwood.

![Image 2: Ncuti Gatwa in Doctor Who series 15 wearing a bowler hat and blue suit](https://www.denofgeek.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Doctor-Who-Ncuti-Gatwa-series-15-bowler-hat-suit.jpg?resize=768%2C432)

_Photo: BBC Studios/Disney/Bad Wolf/Maxine Howells_

In news that will come as comfort to traditionalists, the finale of the current series of _Doctor Who_ (which we’ve stubbornly been calling series 15 for consistency, but almost everywhere else is called season two, so take your pick), won’t be released early on BBC iPlayer. As confirmed on the [official _Doctor Who_ website](https://www.doctorwho.tv/news-and-features/season-2-finale-of-doctor-who-set-for-simultaneous-launch-on-bbc-one-bbc-iplayer), the first time anybody will be able to see the episode will be in an as-yet-unannounced primetime evening BBC One slot on Saturday, May 31. That means no ducking and hiding from potential spoilers in the daytime.

The release strategy means that the episode will be simultaneously available around the world, on BBC One, Disney+ and in the select UK cinemas holding special showings of the current run’s final two episodes, “Wish World”, and “The Reality War”.

Previously, the Disney+-distributed episodes have been made available to stream on BBC iPlayer either at midnight on Fridays (for last year’s series 14) or at 8am on Saturdays (for series 15). Hardcore fans wanting to see the episodes at the earliest opportunity therefore had to stay up late, or get up early and watch them with a bowl of breakfast cereal. Not for the finale.

There are new plot details about that finale, too, straight from showrunner Russell T. Davies:

Ad

Ad – content continues below

_“The Doctor is doomed, Belinda is lost, [Ruby](https://www.doctorwho.tv/characters/ruby-sunday) is trapped, UNIT is powerless, the Unholy Trinity rule supreme and the Underverse is rising. And now we can all experience this devastating climax together, all at the same time, with a unique worldwide premiere. I can promise shocks, scares and revelations off the scale. Come and have fun!”_

Mention of “The Unholy Trinity” and “the Underverse” is a new tease, and makes it sound like the Doctor and co. will be facing suitably god-like forces. Will the mysterious Mrs Flood be among them? Anita Dobson’s character has followed in Susan Triad’s footsteps by popping up in every episode so far this run, and the true nature of her character is destined to be revealed come the finale.

We also heard from actor Millie Gibson on _The One Show_ around the publicity for “Lucky Day” that villainous podcaster Conrad Clark (Jonah Hauer-King) will be returning for the final episode. Could he form one of the Trinity, or is that trio reserved solely for actual deities? Time will tell.

“Wish World” and “The Reality War” are both written by Russell T Davies and directed by Alex Sanjiv Pillai, who also called the shots on the 2024 Christmas special “Joy to the World,” guest-starring Nicola Coughlan and Joel Fry. Find out more about the special _[Doctor Who cinema screenings here](https://www.doctorwho.tv/news-and-features/doctor-who-season-2-finale-coming-to-cinemas-across-the-uk-ireland)_, and read our latest review of Inua Ellams and Makalla McPherson’s episode “The Story and the Engine”, with spoilers, [here](https://www.denofgeek.com/tv/doctor-who-series-15-episode-5-review-the-story-the-engine/).

_Doctor Who airs on Saturdays on BBC One in the UK and streams on Disney+ around the world._

![Image 1](https://cultbox.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Pete-Mctighe-Lucky-Day-TARDIS-Doctor-Who-600x337.jpg)

Posted September 30, 2025 Filed under

While discussing his short story contribution to the _[Doctor Who: Annual 2026](https://cultbox.co.uk/news/books/doctor-who-2026-annual-coming-in-august)_, _Night of the Shreek_ to [The Whoniverse Show](https://youtu.be/zBkbhHljoOw?si=zGjUikvYlVpPpYcn), Pete McTighe described a _Doctor Who_ read-through which became quite rowdy.

**“It was kind of a gift really, being asked to write _Lucky Day_ and to… to kind of come up with the Conrad character because that twist is such a kind of great moment and, you know, the whole time I’m writing the first half of the episode I obviously know that twist is coming. So it’s kind of delicious to have that little secret and to be to be writing and to… give tiny little clues to the audience that… if they go back and watch it a second time they can kind of pick up that, you know, he’s not all he seems.”**

![Image 2](https://cultbox.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Nucti-Gatwa-gasp-Doctor-Who-Lucky-Day-600x337.jpg)

**“I think my favourite thing was the read through where just the gasps that went around the table for, you know, people that hadn’t read the whole script yet. Um, particularly Ncuti \[Gatwa\], just his face and his shock was kind of audible in that moment. And that was yeah, so much fun. It was the most kind of rowdy _Doctor Who_ read through I’ve ever been to.”**

![Image 3](https://cultbox.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Conrad-Think-Tank-Lucky-Day-Season-Two-Doctor-Who-600x337.jpg)

On his short story in the _Doctor Who: Annual 2026_, McTighe fully endorsed host Tyrell Charles’ description of it as a “shreekquel” and explained that the story expands on the past mini adventure that the Doctor and Ruby had while Conrad was secretly observing them.  
**  
“You know, very rarely do you get to revisit a TV episode when you’ve … after you’ve written it. But it was great to kind of dip back in and expand that little bit of the adventure because… I’d always thought that you could do a much bigger story about, you know, Ruby and the Doctor versus the Shreek.”**

![Image 4](https://cultbox.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Doctor-Who-Phial-Ruby-Lucky-Day-Season-Two-600x337.jpg)

**“We needed to focus on Conrad and Ruby and their relationship \[in _Lucky Day_\] and the Doctor was, you know, for obvious reasons, quite sidelined for most of that story. So, you could have done a lot more with it. So doing the short story was just a really great opportunity to do that — and to just spend more time with the doctor and Ruby whom you know are such a great team.”**

Pete McTighe’s _Night of the Shreek_ can be found in the _[Doctor Who: Annual 2026](https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/461666/doctor-who-annual-2026-by-who-doctor/9781405973854)_. An excerpt from it can be found on the official [_Doctor Who_ website](https://www.doctorwho.tv/news-and-features/read-an-exclusive-preview-of-the-doctor-and-rubys-lucky-day-adventure-night-of).

[**_Doctor Who_**](http://screenrant.com/db/tv-show/doctor-who/) season 15 takes a break from Belinda Chandra (Varada Sethu) and The Doctor's (Ncuti Gatwa) long journey home, as the first trailer for episode 4, "Lucky Day," sees season 14 companion Ruby Sunday (Millie Gibson) take charge on Earth. Ruby left the TARDIS at [the end of _Doctor Who_ season 14](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-season-14-ending-explained/) to reconnect with her long-lost family. The new season revolves around the Doctor attempting to return Belinda home to present-day Earth after the TARDIS is prevented from landing, as **the season reveals that something terrible may have taken Earth from history.**

After a terrifying return to a familiar world in "The Well," **the trailer for _Doctor Who_ season 15, episode 4, "Lucky Day," has been released** on [the official _Doctor Who_ YouTube channel](https://youtu.be/Z_DMGSvhofM?si=1Z-z8p65WDnctigO) and brought the series back to Earth.

Reuniting with Ruby Sunday, the episode sees her try to resume a normal life after her time in the TARDIS as she enters a blossoming relationship with Conrad, played by _The Little Mermaid_ star Jonah Hauer-King. However, an inhuman creature is stalking the pair, forcing Ruby to take charge without the aid of the Time Lord.

What "Lucky Day" Means For Doctor Who Season 15's Ongoing Story
---------------------------------------------------------------

### The Doctor May Not Be Reuniting With His Old Friend Just Yet

While season 15's surprising Tenth Doctor sequel took the focus of "The Well," the episode established that **Earth doesn't have a place in the far future**, with humanity having never expanded beyond the stars and the planet itself being unheard of. As such, audiences may be confused to see the Doctor and Belinda seemingly make their way to Earth to meet Ruby, though things may be more complex than they seem.

  ![Image 5: The Doctor (Ncuti Gatwa) and Ruby (Millie Gibson) share a goodbye hug in Doctor Who season 14 episode 8](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/doctor-who-season-14-episode-8-50.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=220&h=182&dpr=2)Related

##### [Why Ruby Sunday Left The TARDIS In Doctor Who Season 14's Ending](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-season-14-why-ruby-left-tardis/ "Why Ruby Sunday Left The TARDIS In Doctor Who Season 14's Ending")

The reason Doctor Who's Ruby Sunday stayed on Earth at the end of season 14 instead of continuing to go on new adventures with the Doctor.

Posts[](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-season-14-why-ruby-left-tardis/#threads "Total Posts")

By  [Jack Ori](https://screenrant.com/author/jack-ori/ "Posts by Jack Ori")

In the brief glimpses that show Ruby and the Doctor together, they are wearing the outfits seen in "The Church on Ruby Road" and "Space Babies," which **hints that there may be unseen moments between either adventure**. Furthermore, the Doctor and Belinda may once more be stuck in the past and unable to progress to May 25, 2025, but their actions may reverberate into Ruby's present-day adventure. As such, her upcoming adventure will still be a showcase of how she has grown since leading the Time Lord.

Our Thoughts On Doctor Who Season 15's "Lucky Day" Trailer
----------------------------------------------------------

### Something Is Troubling The Doctor's Closest Allies In His Absence

   ![Image 6: Doctor Who Season 15 Lucky Day Millie Gibson and Jonah Hauer King as Ruby and Conrad Date](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/doctor-who-season-15-lucky-day-millie-gibson-and-jonah-hauer-king-as-ruby-and-conrad-date.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2)

Doctor Who Season 15 Lucky Day Millie Gibson and Jonah Hauer King as Ruby and Conrad Date

**_Doctor Who_** season 15 has so far kept the fate of Earth a mystery, with "The Well" only just beginning to address its absence from the universe. As such, many mainstays of Russell T Davies' second tenure, [such as his friends at UNIT](https://screenrant.com/doctor-who-unit-team-members-explained/), have strangely been absent. Early on-set pictures teased a storyline that saw the organization forced to reckon with a public that had become more skeptical of their handling of extraterrestrial threats. As such, Ruby taking the lead in a Doctor-lite adventure may be a perfect opportunity to explore how Earth fares in his absence.
